title: Scarcity and production possibilities
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: Scarcity requires choosing among competing uses of resources. A production frontier shows efficient combinations with fixed resources and technology. Moving along it changes the output mix; moving outward requires expanded productive capacity. Opportunity cost is the next-best forgone alternative. A point inside the frontier can reflect unemployment or inefficient resource use, so an economy can increase current output without moving its frontier.
formula: Opportunity cost = output forgone / output gained
steps: An economy reallocates resources from 50 units of food and 10 machines to 38 food and 14 machines.
It gains four machines and gives up 12 food.
The opportunity cost over the interval is three food per machine.
This movement changes the mix, not the economy’s production frontier.
trap: Growth of current output from an interior point need not mean growth of productive capacity.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: An economy reallocates resources from 50 units of food and 10 machines to 38 food and 14 machines. It gains four machines and gives up 12 food. The opportunity cost over the interval is three food per machine. This movement changes the mix, not the economy’s production frontier. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

questions.hint: Growth of current output from an interior point need not mean growth of productive capacity.
questions.explain: An attainable point inside the frontier.

title: Specialization and the terms of trade
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: Comparative advantage depends on relative opportunity costs; absolute advantage depends on productivity. A country with lower opportunity cost in a good can specialize in that good and trade at terms between the countries’ opportunity costs. This can expand consumption possibilities without shifting production possibilities. It does not guarantee equal gains for every person or eliminate adjustment costs. State whether the data describe output per resource or resources per output before comparing.
formula: A mutually beneficial exchange rate lies between opportunity costs
steps: A can make 20 cloth or 10 grain per day; B can make 12 cloth or 12 grain.
A’s opportunity cost of grain is two cloth; B’s is one cloth.
B has comparative advantage in grain.
At 1.5 cloth per grain, B gains relative to domestic production and A saves relative to its own grain cost.
trap: Do not reverse the ratio when moving between output data and input-time data.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: A can make 20 cloth or 10 grain per day; B can make 12 cloth or 12 grain. A’s opportunity cost of grain is two cloth; B’s is one cloth. B has comparative advantage in grain. At 1.5 cloth per grain, B gains relative to domestic production and A saves relative to its own grain cost. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

questions.hint: Do not reverse the ratio when moving between output data and input-time data.

title: Demand and supply as separate decisions
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: A demand curve describes purchases at different own prices, holding other influences fixed. A supply curve describes sales on the same basis. Income and preferences can shift demand; input costs and technology can shift supply. A change in the good’s own price moves along a curve. The market model is a starting point for relative-price reasoning; the economy-wide aggregate demand model later uses different mechanisms.
formula: Own-price change → movement; nonprice determinant change → shift
steps: A production technology reduces unit cost.
At each price firms now offer more, so supply shifts right.
With demand unchanged, equilibrium price falls and quantity rises.
The lower price causes movement along demand, not a demand shift.
trap: Do not call every increase in purchases an increase in demand.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: A production technology reduces unit cost. At each price firms now offer more, so supply shifts right. With demand unchanged, equilibrium price falls and quantity rises. The lower price causes movement along demand, not a demand shift. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

title: Equilibrium and simultaneous shifts
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: At equilibrium planned purchases equal planned sales. Below the equilibrium price, a shortage tends to push price upward; above it, a surplus tends to push price downward. A new equilibrium can be traced after a curve shifts. When supply and demand shift together, a direction can be uncertain: increases in both raise quantity, but their effects on price oppose one another. Graph both changes before deciding which outcomes are determinate.
formula: Set Qd = Qs, or inverse demand price = inverse supply price
steps: Demand is P = 70 − Q and supply is P = 10 + Q.
Equating them gives 2Q = 60.
Equilibrium quantity is 30 and price is 40.
A rightward demand shift with supply fixed raises both price and quantity.
trap: A shortage is a quantity difference at a specified price, not a shift of demand.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: Demand is P = 70 − Q and supply is P = 10 + Q. Equating them gives 2Q = 60. Equilibrium quantity is 30 and price is 40. A rightward demand shift with supply fixed raises both price and quantity. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

part: Economic Indicators and the Business Cycle
title: GDP, circular flow and what is omitted
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: GDP measures the market value of final goods and services produced within an economy during a period. Spending on domestic production becomes income to producers. Count final production once: intermediate inputs are already embodied in final value. Transfers and transactions in existing financial assets are not purchases of current production. GDP omits many nonmarket activities and does not directly measure distribution, leisure or environmental quality, so it is not a complete welfare measure.
formula: GDP = C + I + G + (X − M)
steps: Consumption is 500, investment 100, government purchases 150, exports 80 and imports 60.
Net exports are 20.
Imports are subtracted to remove foreign production already included in other spending categories, not because imports are inherently harmful.
trap: Government transfers are not government purchases in GDP.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: Consumption is 500, investment 100, government purchases 150, exports 80 and imports 60. Net exports are 20. GDP is 500 + 100 + 150 + 20 = 770. Imports are subtracted to remove foreign production already included in other spending categories, not because imports are inherently harmful. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

part: Economic Indicators and the Business Cycle
title: Labor force and unemployment
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: The labor force consists of employed people and unemployed people actively seeking work under the measurement definition. The unemployment rate uses the labor force, not the entire population, as its denominator. Discouraged workers who stop searching leave the labor force and can make the measured unemployment rate fall without more employment. Frictional and structural unemployment remain at the natural rate; cyclical unemployment is associated with deviations from full-employment output.
formula: Unemployment rate = unemployed / labor force × 100%; participation = labor force / eligible population × 100%
steps: There are 180 employed people and 20 unemployed active job seekers.
The labor force is 200.
The unemployment rate is 20 / 200 × 100 = 10%.
If some discouraged workers stop searching, interpret the lower rate alongside participation rather than assuming employment rose.
trap: Someone without a job is not automatically classified as unemployed.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: There are 180 employed people and 20 unemployed active job seekers. The labor force is 200. The unemployment rate is 20 / 200 × 100 = 10%. If some discouraged workers stop searching, interpret the lower rate alongside participation rather than assuming employment rose. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

part: Economic Indicators and the Business Cycle
title: Price indices, inflation and real output
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: A price index compares the cost of a specified basket or set of production weights across time. Inflation is the percentage change in the index, not its level. Nominal GDP uses current prices; real GDP removes price changes using base-period valuation or the relevant chained method. Unexpected inflation redistributes purchasing power between parties to fixed nominal contracts; borrowers can gain while lenders lose when inflation exceeds expectations. A slowing inflation rate still means prices rise if inflation remains positive.
formula: Inflation = (new index − old index) / old index × 100%; real GDP = nominal GDP / (deflator / 100)
steps: The price index rises from 120 to 126.
The increase is 6 relative to the old index 120.
Inflation is 5%.
If nominal GDP is 630 and the GDP deflator is 126, real GDP is 630 / 1.26 = 500.
trap: A decline in inflation from 6% to 3% is disinflation, not deflation.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: The price index rises from 120 to 126. The increase is 6 relative to the old index 120. Inflation is 5%. If nominal GDP is 630 and the GDP deflator is 126, real GDP is 630 / 1.26 = 500. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

part: Economic Indicators and the Business Cycle
title: Expansion, contraction and turning points
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: The business cycle alternates expansion and contraction in real economic activity. Peaks and troughs are turning points between those phases. An expansion does not require every household’s income to rise; a contraction does not mean all prices must fall. Potential output is a sustainable benchmark rather than a rigid maximum. Compare real output with potential and changes over time separately: output can grow while still below potential.
formula: Output gap = (actual real output − potential output) / potential output × 100%
steps: Potential output is 1000 while actual output rises from 900 to 950.
The economy is expanding over this interval.
Actual output remains below potential.
Its gap at 950 is (950 − 1000) / 1000 × 100 = −5%, so growth alone does not prove full employment.
trap: Peaks and troughs are turning points; expansion and contraction are the cycle’s phases.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: Potential output is 1000 while actual output rises from 900 to 950. The economy is expanding over this interval. Actual output remains below potential. Its gap at 950 is (950 − 1000) / 1000 × 100 = −5%, so growth alone does not prove full employment. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

questions.hint: Peaks and troughs are turning points; expansion and contraction are the cycle’s phases.
questions.explain: An expansion occurs alongside a negative output gap.

title: Aggregate demand and the simple multiplier
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: Aggregate demand shows desired total spending on domestic final output at different price levels. Its downward slope reflects wealth, interest-rate and exchange-rate channels rather than the single-good substitution story. Autonomous spending shifts AD. In the simple closed-economy model without taxes, imports, price changes or crowding out, repeated spending makes the total output response exceed the initial change. Real-world responses depend on leakages and supply conditions.
formula: Simple spending multiplier = 1 / (1 − MPC); tax multiplier = −MPC / (1 − MPC)
steps: Households spend 0.75 of extra income.
The simple spending multiplier is 1 / 0.25 = 4.
An autonomous purchase increase of 20 raises equilibrium output by 80 under the stated assumptions.
A tax cut of 20 has a smaller initial consumption effect, so its simple total effect is 60.
trap: Do not apply the simple multiplier as an unconditional forecast when prices or interest rates change.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: Households spend 0.75 of extra income. The simple spending multiplier is 1 / 0.25 = 4. An autonomous purchase increase of 20 raises equilibrium output by 80 under the stated assumptions. A tax cut of 20 has a smaller initial consumption effect, so its simple total effect is 60. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

questions.hint: Do not apply the simple multiplier as an unconditional forecast when prices or interest rates change.
questions.explain: Some of the tax change is initially saved.

title: Short-run supply and equilibrium shocks
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: SRAS slopes upward when some input prices or expectations adjust slowly. LRAS is vertical at potential output in the benchmark model. AD–AS equilibrium determines real output and the price level. A negative supply shock shifts SRAS left, raising prices while lowering output: a demand expansion does not create this same combination by itself. Identify the curve, direction and horizon before predicting output, unemployment and prices.
formula: AD increase with SRAS fixed → higher short-run output and price level
steps: An energy cost shock raises firms’ production costs.
SRAS shifts left with AD held fixed.
The price level rises and real output falls in the short run.
Cyclical unemployment rises; this combination is often called stagflation.
trap: A change in the price level is movement along AD, not an AD shift by itself.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: An energy cost shock raises firms’ production costs. SRAS shifts left with AD held fixed. The price level rises and real output falls in the short run. Cyclical unemployment rises; this combination is often called stagflation. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

questions.explain: Raises the price level and lowers real output.

title: Long-run self-adjustment
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: Following a demand shock, short-run output can differ from potential because nominal wages and other input prices adjust slowly. In a recessionary gap, downward pressure on wages can lower costs and shift SRAS right over time. In an inflationary gap, rising wages can shift SRAS left. If productive capacity is unchanged, the long-run benchmark returns output to LRAS. The speed and costs of adjustment are separate empirical questions.
formula: Demand shock alone with fixed potential output: long-run real output returns to potential
steps: AD falls while wages initially remain sticky.
Output falls below potential and unemployment rises.
Over time lower nominal wages reduce production costs, shifting SRAS right.
Output returns toward potential at a lower price level, assuming no lasting supply-side damage.
trap: LRAS does not automatically move just because AD has shifted.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: AD falls while wages initially remain sticky. Output falls below potential and unemployment rises. Over time lower nominal wages reduce production costs, shifting SRAS right. Output returns toward potential at a lower price level, assuming no lasting supply-side damage. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

questions.explain: Falling input costs shift SRAS right over time.

title: Fiscal actions and automatic stabilizers
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: Expansionary fiscal policy raises government purchases or reduces taxes to support AD; contractionary policy works in the opposite direction. Automatic stabilizers operate through existing rules: in downturns, tax receipts fall and some transfer payments rise without new legislation. Timing, crowding out and supply conditions can limit the effect of discretionary action. Distinguish a change in government purchases from a transfer-induced change in consumption.
formula: Simple model: ΔY = spending multiplier × ΔG
steps: A recessionary gap is 100 in a fixed-price model with MPC 0.75.
The spending multiplier is 4.
An increase in government purchases of 25 could close the gap under the model’s assumptions.
Existing unemployment benefits can separately cushion disposable income without being counted directly as G in GDP.
trap: Automatic stabilizers do not require a new discretionary vote for each downturn.

An increase in government purchases of 25 could close the gap under the model’s assumptions. title: Assets, bond prices and real returns
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: Financial assets are claims on future payments. A bond’s fixed payments become less attractive when market interest rates rise, so its price falls. Stocks represent ownership rather than a promised fixed payment. The nominal interest rate is stated in money terms; the real interest rate adjusts for inflation. The common subtraction formula is an approximation; the exact relationship uses a ratio. Expected inflation matters when contracts are set, while realized inflation determines the ex post real return.
formula: Approximate real interest rate = nominal rate − inflation rate
steps: A one-year nominal rate is 7% and expected inflation is 3%.
The approximate expected real rate is 4%.
If actual inflation turns out to be 5%, the approximate realized real rate is 2%.
For a fixed future bond payment, a higher discount rate lowers its current price.
trap: Do not confuse a bond’s price with its interest yield; they move oppositely for fixed payments.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: A one-year nominal rate is 7% and expected inflation is 3%. The approximate expected real rate is 4%. If actual inflation turns out to be 5%, the approximate realized real rate is 2%. For a fixed future bond payment, a higher discount rate lowers its current price. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

title: Money, bank balance sheets and deposit creation
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: Money functions as a medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value. Bank reserves are bank assets, while customer deposits are bank liabilities. Lending can create deposits, subject to constraints and the monetary framework. The textbook reciprocal-reserve multiplier gives a maximum under restrictive assumptions: all excess reserves are lent and loans redeposit with no cash leakage. It is not a universal description of actual banking, particularly in an ample-reserves system.
formula: Textbook maximum deposit multiplier = 1 / reserve ratio, under stated assumptions
steps: A bank receives a new cash deposit of 100 and the assumed required reserve ratio is 20%.
It must retain 20 and can initially lend 80 if it holds no excess reserves.
With full redepositing and repeated maximum lending, total deposits can reach 500 from that new reserve injection.
The maximum additional loans are 400; distinguish total deposits from additional lending.
trap: The initial deposit is included in total deposits; do not count it twice or assume the theoretical maximum is guaranteed.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: A bank receives a new cash deposit of 100 and the assumed required reserve ratio is 20%. It must retain 20 and can initially lend 80 if it holds no excess reserves. With full redepositing and repeated maximum lending, total deposits can reach 500 from that new reserve injection. The maximum additional loans are 400; distinguish total deposits from additional lending. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

title: Monetary policy with limited and ample reserves
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: The traditional money-market model relates a nominal interest rate to money demand and a fixed nominal money supply. Under limited reserves, reserve-supply changes can move an overnight rate along reserve demand. Under ample reserves, administered rates such as interest on reserves are central tools for steering short-term rates; changing reserve quantity alone may have little effect within the flat region. Lower policy rates can support interest-sensitive spending, but transmission is neither immediate nor guaranteed.
formula: Expansionary rate policy → lower short-term rates → more interest-sensitive spending, other things equal
steps: A central bank operating with ample reserves lowers its administered rates.
This lowers incentives to hold or lend reserves at previously higher rates.
Market short-term rates tend to move down.
Lower borrowing rates can increase investment and consumption, shifting AD right if other influences are unchanged.
trap: Do not assume every bond purchase lowers rates equally in an ample-reserves regime.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: A central bank operating with ample reserves lowers its administered rates. This lowers incentives to hold or lend reserves at previously higher rates. Market short-term rates tend to move down. Lower borrowing rates can increase investment and consumption, shifting AD right if other influences are unchanged. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

title: Saving, investment and loanable funds
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: The loanable-funds model relates the real interest rate to desired saving and borrowing. More saving shifts supply right, lowering the equilibrium real rate and increasing funds exchanged. Higher expected investment returns shift demand right. Government borrowing can increase demand for loanable funds and raise the real rate under stated assumptions. Specify the diagram’s convention: some presentations instead model reduced national saving as a supply shift. Do not shift both for the same event.
formula: Loanable-funds equilibrium: saving supplied = borrowing demanded at a real interest rate
steps: Expected returns to new capital improve.
Firms seek more borrowing at each real interest rate.
Loanable-funds demand shifts right while saving supply is unchanged.
The real rate and equilibrium funds rise in this closed-economy comparison.
trap: The money market uses a nominal rate; the loanable-funds model uses a real rate.
challenge: Reconstruct the worked example on paper. Label the quantities or graph axes, explain each causal step, then state one assumption that could change the result.
solution: A complete explanation should include these links: Expected returns to new capital improve. Firms seek more borrowing at each real interest rate. Loanable-funds demand shifts right while saving supply is unchanged. The real rate and equilibrium funds rise in this closed-economy comparison. State the model assumptions; the example is not a forecast or an observed result.

options: Lower the real rate and raise funds exchanged.
Raise the real rate and lower funds exchanged.
Shift borrowing demand left automatically.
Eliminate investment.
questions.hint: The money market uses a nominal rate; the loanable-funds model uses a real rate.
questions.explain: Lower the real rate and raise funds exchanged.

title: Stabilization and the Phillips curve
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: In the short run, AD changes can create an inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment along a given short-run Phillips curve. Changes in expected inflation or supply conditions shift that curve. The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural unemployment rate in the benchmark; there is no permanent inflation-unemployment tradeoff from repeatedly surprising people with higher inflation. A supply shock can worsen both inflation and unemployment, so the short-run curve is not a universal fixed law.
formula: AD expansion: move toward higher inflation and lower unemployment on a given SRPC

title: Money growth and long-run inflation
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: The quantity equation relates the money stock, its velocity, the price level and real output. It is an identity when velocity is defined consistently. Predicting inflation from money growth requires assumptions about velocity and real output growth. In the long-run classical benchmark, sustained money growth beyond real output growth raises inflation if velocity is stable; changes in nominal variables alone do not permanently raise productive capacity. Short-run money demand and supply responses can complicate this relationship.
formula: MV = PY; approximate inflation = money growth + velocity growth − real output growth
steps: Money grows 6%, velocity is stable and real output grows 2%.
The approximate growth-rate equation gives inflation of 4%.
This result depends on stable velocity.
If velocity falls, the same money growth can coexist with lower inflation, so inspect assumptions before applying the shortcut.
trap: The quantity equation by itself does not prove velocity is constant.

title: Deficits, debt and crowding out
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: A deficit is a flow: government outlays exceed revenues during a period. Debt is a stock of accumulated borrowing subject to repayments and other accounting changes. In the closed-economy loanable-funds model with saving behavior held fixed, more government borrowing can raise real interest rates and reduce private investment. This crowding-out effect can offset some short-run fiscal stimulus and affect future capital formation. Its size depends on conditions, including monetary response and foreign capital.
formula: Deficit = outlays − revenues; simplified next debt = current debt + deficit
steps: Government outlays are 300 and revenues 260.
The deficit is 40.
If initial debt is 500 with no other changes, next debt is 540.
If the borrowing raises real rates, some interest-sensitive private investment can be crowded out; the deficit is not the same number as total debt.
trap: A smaller positive deficit still adds to debt in this simplified accounting.

solution: A complete explanation should include these links: Government outlays are 300 and revenues 260. The deficit is 40. If initial debt is 500 with no other changes, next debt is 540. title: Growth and productive capacity
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: Long-run growth in real output per person depends on productivity, capital, human skills, technology and institutions. A larger labor force can raise total output without raising output per person. Saving and investment can expand physical capital; education and research can raise human capital or technology. Policy comparisons must consider opportunity costs, incentives and implementation rather than treating any spending label as guaranteed growth. Growth shifts LRAS and the production frontier outward.
formula: Real GDP per capita = real GDP / population
steps: Real output is 1200 and population is 100.
Output per person is 12.

Output per person remains 12, so total growth did not increase the per-person measure in this example.
trap: A temporary AD expansion is not the same as a rise in long-run productive capacity.

title: International transactions and accounting
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: The current account records trade in goods and services plus relevant income and transfer flows. The financial account records transactions in financial assets. A current-account deficit is associated with offsetting financing flows under consistent accounting conventions, allowing for capital-account items and statistical discrepancies. Some presentations describe capital inflow as positive financing even when official asset/liability sign conventions differ. State the convention and identify the real transaction before assigning a sign.
formula: Trade balance = exports − imports; current account includes more than trade
steps: Exports are 80 and imports 100, so the trade balance is −20.
Assume no net income or transfers and no other accounting items.
The current account is then −20.
It is financed by an offsetting net financial inflow of 20 using the inflow-positive classroom convention.

title: Exchange-rate quotations and currency demand
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in another; every graph and calculation needs an explicit quotation. If the domestic currency buys more foreign currency, it appreciates. Foreign purchases of domestic goods or assets can increase demand for domestic currency. Domestic purchases abroad can increase its supply in the foreign-exchange market. Supply and demand refer to the currency named on the graph, not to an unspecified country in general.
formula: Foreign-currency cost = domestic amount × foreign units per domestic unit
steps: The exchange rate is 0.8 foreign units per domestic unit.

If the domestic currency appreciates to 1 foreign unit per domestic unit, the same item costs the buyer 50.
The item becomes more expensive in foreign currency with its domestic price fixed.

title: Policy, interest differences and capital flows
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: Other things equal, a higher domestic real interest rate relative to foreign rates can attract financial inflows as investors seek returns. Demand for domestic currency can rise and the currency can appreciate under a floating exchange rate. Expectations and risk can change the result, so the interest differential alone is not a guaranteed forecast. Trace the policy to the interest rate and then to the named currency’s demand rather than jumping directly to exports.

Foreign investors seek more domestic assets.
Demand for domestic currency shifts right.
The currency appreciates in a floating market; this can reduce net exports later through relative prices.

title: Net exports and open-economy transmission
goal: Explain the mechanism, work through an example, and test your reasoning.
idea: Domestic currency appreciation makes domestic goods more costly to foreign buyers and foreign goods cheaper to domestic buyers, holding nominal product prices fixed. Exports tend to fall and imports tend to rise, reducing net exports and AD in the simplified model. Depreciation tends to work in reverse. The response depends on elasticities, contracts and adjustment lags, so immediate trade balances need not follow the eventual direction. Exchange-rate effects can offset or reinforce domestic policy.
formula: Net exports = X − M; appreciation tends to reduce NX, other things equal
steps: A currency appreciation occurs with domestic and foreign goods prices fixed.
Exports in the example fall from 100 to 90 while imports rise from 80 to 85.
Net exports fall from 20 to 5.
The net-export component of AD falls by 15; a multiplier effect requires additional assumptions.
trap: Do not confuse cheaper imports for domestic buyers with a guaranteed rise in domestic net exports.
